item.title: My simple fix for the messed up Sunday Shows
item.description: Rosen finds Sunday talk shows frustrating due to their format, repetitive political guests, and focus on Washington D.C. Their simple fix involves changing the format to feature one non-politician guest for a one-on-one interview followed by a round table discussion with experts, eliminating politicians. Rosen suggests moving the show's location out of Washington D.C. to reflect the country better and broadcasting it throughout the week on various platforms to reach a wider audience. These changes aim to make the shows more engaging and informative by focusing on issues rather than political maneuvering.

item.title: How to Know If You Are Behaving Ethically as a Journalist: Jay Rosen’s Checklist
item.description: Jay Rosen's checklist offers a framework for ethical journalism, focusing on the impact of actions rather than perfect moral behavior. The checklist, developed for students and newsrooms, comprises eight key components: transparency regarding methods and motives; admitting and correcting mistakes; involving the community in newsgathering; showing empathy and humanity towards subjects; actively listening to audiences and sources; ensuring fairness and proportionality in reporting; practicing humility and self-doubt; and demonstrating courage. These principles aim to guide journalists in adapting their ethical practices amidst changes in the field, encouraging accountability and a rational, transparent approach to reporting.

item.title: Why I Don’t Trust a Thing the Church of the Savvy Says About Candidate Obama’s Call for Transparency
item.description: Rosen reflects on a conversation about Obama's call for transparency and expresses skepticism about its feasibility given the political system's reliance on secrecy. They are concerned that the same people who initially praised Obama's transparency call are now defending the White House's spin tactics, questioning the Church of the Savvy's stance on the issue. Rosen believes that prioritizing the perceived greater good can erode transparency over time, making them distrustful of any statements made on the topic by this group.

item.title: What I Told the Man from Politics Daily
item.description: The Republican Party in Texas faces internal challenges, despite its history of electoral success. The party struggles with a primary problem, as run-offs often push the party toward extremes, silencing moderate voices. Moderate Republicans sometimes vote in the Democratic primary. However, the party's conservative principles, like low taxes and regulations, remain popular, and the state's growing population brings in new conservative voters. The Republican Party can succeed in Texas by addressing the primary issues and re-integrating moderate viewpoints. The future of the party in Texas is promising, but requires effort.

item.title: Mediabistro on Rosen and Shirky
item.description: Five years ago, Shirky stated, newspapers were losing readership left and right, but their revenue was booming. Ironically, now most newspapers actually have more readers due to their Web sites, but the money has dried up. Starting (debatably) as early as Dan Rather ’s MemoGate in 2004, and up to the recent Balloon Boy incident, the Internet has offered up information that contradicts what is being fed to us by our televisions or newspapers.

item.title: What Are Journalism Schools For?
item.description: Studio 20 Professor Jay Rosen responds in a GRITtv interview with Laura Flanders: “In the past, journalism schools have always been able to train people in skills for slots in stable media empires, and now those empires are crumbling. So, what we need to do in journalism school is engage our students in the puzzle of what the next journalism system looks like and teach them to be innovators and entrepreneurs and to start their own systems, but also to help the old media to figure out how to renew itself. So, that’s what we’re trying to do.” Watch the full video: 2 notes

item.title: Sources of subsidy in the production of news: a list
item.description: The economics of the news business involves various subsidies because news production is often not profitable on its own. Jay Rosen poses the question of what are the main and emerging sources of these subsidies. Examples include unpaid citizen labor, foundation grants, corporate underwriting, government support, losses absorbed by news organizations, profits from related companies, and advertising revenue. Rosen seeks input from readers to compile a comprehensive list of these subsidies, which are essential for the existence of the news system as it is known.

item.title: Is "He Said, She Said, We're Clueless" Coverage Dying?
item.description: The author critiques Jay Rosen's optimistic view on the decline of "he said, she said" journalism. While acknowledging that sophisticated journalists recognize the flaws of false balance, the author argues that economic pressures in the media industry, including job cuts and the loss of specialized journalists, make the lazy shortcut of "he said, she said" reporting even more prevalent. The author concludes that the blogosphere's ability to counteract this trend is limited due to the underlying economic realities of the media business.
